sprints.title: Repo Scout — GitHub API scraper for cybersecurity education repos
sprints.notes: Build the primary GitHub scraper using the GitHub Search API. Search strategies: (1) Topic-based search — query repos tagged with: cybersecurity, ethical-hacking, infosec, penetration-testing, ctf, network-security, cloud-security, malware-analysis, digital-forensics, incident-response, oscp, ceh, comptia, security-plus, ccna, sysadmin, linux-administration, windows-server. (2) Keyword search — search repo names and descriptions for: 'course', 'curriculum', 'slides', 'lecture', 'lab', 'workshop', 'bootcamp', 'training', 'educational', 'learning-path', 'study-guide', 'certification', 'exam-prep'. (3) Awesome-list mining — scrape awesome-cybersecurity, awesome-hacking, awesome-pentest, awesome-security, awesome-infosec and similar curated lists for linked repos. (4) Organization scanning — scan known edu orgs: OWASP, SANS, NIST repos, university CS departments with public course materials. (5) User-based — find prolific cybersecurity educators on GitHub and scan their repos. Filters: minimum 10 stars, has license file, last updated within 2 years, contains markdown/HTML/PDF/PPTX content (not just code tools). Output: per-repo JSON record with metadata, content preview, and Hexworth house recommendation. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js scan --topic cybersecurity --min-stars 10.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — GitLab and alternative platform scrapers
sprints.notes: Extend Repo Scout beyond GitHub to other platforms. GitLab: use GitLab API (v4) to search public projects with cybersecurity/education topics. Many university courses host on GitLab (self-hosted instances and gitlab.com). Bitbucket: search public repos — less common for edu content but some exist. SourceHut: niche but growing, some security research hosted here. Academic sources: (1) MIT OpenCourseWare — scrape course listings for computer science and cybersecurity, find linked GitHub repos or downloadable materials. (2) Coursera/edX — identify open-source companion repos for security courses. (3) Open Textbook Library — search for CC-licensed cybersecurity and networking textbooks. (4) Archive.org — search for archived educational materials with permissive licenses. Non-repo content sources: (5) SlideShare/SpeakerDeck — scrape for cybersecurity presentation decks with CC licenses. (6) NIST/CISA public resources — training materials, frameworks, guides (all public domain). Each platform gets its own scraper module under _tools/repo-scout/scrapers/. Common output format so all discoveries feed into the same manifest.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Content classifier and house mapper
sprints.notes: Build an automated classifier that analyzes discovered repos and maps them to Hexworth houses. Analysis steps: (1) File type inventory — count markdown, HTML, PPTX, PDF, Jupyter notebooks, YAML, code files to determine content type (lecture slides, labs, reference docs, tools). (2) Keyword extraction — scan README and top-level docs for domain keywords: map to houses using keyword → house lookup table (e.g., 'firewall' → shield/web, 'malware' → dark-arts, 'AWS' → cloud, 'subnet' → web, 'Arduino' → forge, 'Python' → code, 'cryptography' → key, 'SIEM' → eye, 'PowerShell' → script). (3) License classifier — categorize license permissiveness (Public Domain > CC0 > MIT > Apache 2.0 > CC-BY > CC-BY-SA > GPL > CC-BY-NC > proprietary/unknown). Flag non-commercial licenses as 'review required'. (4) Quality scoring — composite score based on: stars, forks, recency, content volume, file organization, README quality, license permissiveness. (5) Conversion effort estimator — small (< 10 files, simple markdown), medium (10-50 files, mixed formats), large (50+ files or complex PPTX/PDF conversion). Output: enriched discovery record with house[], contentType, license, qualityScore, conversionEffort, recommended priority. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js classify --input discoveries.json.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Discovery dashboard and review workflow
sprints.notes: Build a dashboard to review, approve, and track discovered repos. Features: (1) Discovery browser — filterable/sortable table of all discovered repos: name, URL, house mapping, quality score, license, conversion effort, status (new/reviewed/approved/forked/converting/converted/rejected). (2) Review workflow — click a discovery to see full details: README preview, file tree, content samples, license text, similar repos already in pipeline. Mark as 'approve for fork', 'reject' (with reason), or 'bookmark for later'. (3) Fork tracker — once approved, track the fork process: forked → content extracted → conversion sprint created → conversion in progress → integrated into Prime. (4) Stats dashboard — total discoveries, by house, by license, by status, conversion pipeline metrics. (5) Scheduled scanning — configure cron/scheduled task to run scrapers weekly and surface new discoveries. (6) Duplicate detection — flag repos that contain substantially similar content to already-forked repos or existing Prime content. Build as HTML page in _tools/repo-scout/dashboard.html or as CLI reports: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js dashboard, node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js report --format md.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Auto-fork and content extraction pipeline
sprints.notes: Automate the fork → extract → stage pipeline. Auto-fork: use GitHub API (or gh CLI) to fork approved repos to the FM-256 GitHub organization. Naming convention: hexworth-source-{original-repo-name}. Content extraction: (1) Clone the forked repo locally to _planning/repo-scout-imports/{repo-name}/. (2) Extract convertible content — PPTX files (use python-pptx to extract text + images), PDF files (extract text with PyMuPDF/pdfplumber), Markdown files (copy directly), Jupyter notebooks (extract cells), HTML slides (copy directly). (3) Generate a conversion manifest: source file → target Prime file mapping, with house assignment and module numbering. (4) Auto-create sprint items — for each repo, generate EHE-style sprint items in sprints.json for the conversion work (one item per module/chapter). Safeguards: never auto-fork without approval flag, never overwrite existing Prime content, always preserve attribution and license in extracted content. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js fork RS-{id}, node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js extract {repo-name}.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — License compliance and attribution tracker
sprints.notes: Build a license compliance system to ensure all forked and converted content respects original licenses. Components: (1) License database — for every forked repo, store: original license text, license type (SPDX identifier), original author(s), original URL, fork date, any license conditions (attribution required, share-alike, non-commercial). (2) Attribution generator — automatically generate attribution notices for converted content. Each Prime module converted from external source gets a footer or metadata field: 'Adapted from [Original Title] by [Author], licensed under [License]. Original: [URL]'. (3) License compatibility matrix — which licenses allow what: can we modify? must we share-alike? can we use commercially? must we attribute? (4) Compliance checker — scan _planning/repo-scout-imports/ and cross-reference with license database, flag any content lacking license info or using incompatible licenses. (5) NOTICE file — maintain a master NOTICE.md listing all third-party content sources, licenses, and attribution. This is non-negotiable — protects Hexworth legally and respects open-source community. Store at _tools/repo-scout/licenses.json and generate NOTICE.md.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Conversion template engine for common formats
sprints.notes: Build reusable conversion templates to speed up the raw-to-Prime pipeline. Templates needed: (1) PPTX → Presentation HTML — extract slides from PowerPoint, convert to Prime slide-based presentation format with correct house theme (auto-detect house from RS-4 classification). Handle: text extraction, bullet points, images (export to assets/), tables, code blocks, speaker notes. (2) Markdown → Presentation HTML — convert structured markdown (headings = slides) to Prime presentation format. (3) PDF → Presentation HTML — extract pages/sections, OCR if scanned, convert to slides. (4) Jupyter Notebook → Lab HTML — convert notebook cells to Prime interactive lab format. (5) Quiz/Test Bank → Quiz HTML — parse common test bank formats (CSV, QTI, Respondus, plain text Q&A) into Prime quiz format. Each template: auto-applies correct house color palette, adds Hexworth navigation chrome, generates content-registry.js entry stub, creates progress tracking hooks. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/convert.js --input source.pptx --house dark-arts --module-id ehe-01 --type presentation. This is the force multiplier — makes bulk conversion feasible instead of hand-building every module.

sprints.title: Repo Scout — Initial seed scan and first batch fork
sprints.notes: Run the first production scan and fork the initial batch of high-value repos. Target: 50-100 discovered repos, fork top 10-20 highest-quality finds. Priority search targets by house: Dark Arts (ethical hacking courses, CTF writeup collections, pentest methodology repos), Web (networking courses, CCNA/Network+ study materials, protocol labs), Cloud (AWS/Azure/GCP security courses, cloud architecture materials), Code (programming courses with security focus, algorithm visualizations), Shield (GRC frameworks, compliance guides, risk assessment templates), Key (cryptography courses, crypto challenge sets), Eye (SIEM/SOC training materials, log analysis courses, threat hunting playbooks), Script (automation courses, scripting tutorials, DevOps security), Forge (hardware hacking, IoT security, embedded systems courses). Deliverable: first discoveries.json populated, first batch of forks completed, conversion sprints auto-generated for top 5 repos. This proves the pipeline end-to-end and starts feeding fresh content into the conversion queue.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Hardware inventory, drive assessment, and BIOS/UEFI setup
sprints.notes: Physical setup and inventory of the Neon main server. Tasks: (1) Document hardware specs — CPU, RAM (total and configuration), motherboard model, NIC(s), GPU if any, PSU wattage. (2) Inventory all hard drives — make, model, capacity, interface (SATA, NVMe, SAS), current health (SMART data), RPM/type (HDD vs SSD). (3) Decide drive layout strategy: which drive(s) for OS, which for data/databases, which for backups, any hot spares. (4) BIOS/UEFI configuration — boot order, enable virtualization (VT-x/AMD-V, VT-d/IOMMU if needed), AHCI mode for SATA, NVMe configuration, fan/thermal settings, wake-on-LAN if desired. (5) Check/update firmware — BIOS, drive firmware, NIC firmware, RAID controller firmware if applicable. (6) Physical setup — rack/shelf placement, power connections (UPS if available), network cabling (at least 1 Gbps, ideally 2.5/10G if hardware supports), KVM or remote management (IPMI/iLO/iDRAC if server-grade). Deliverable: hardware manifest document and drive layout plan approved before OS install.

sprints.title: Neon Server — OS installation and base system configuration
sprints.notes: Install and configure the base operating system on Neon. Decisions: (1) OS selection — Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (stable, wide support, 5-year maintenance), Debian 12 (rock-solid, minimal), Rocky Linux 9 / AlmaLinux 9 (RHEL-based, enterprise), or Proxmox VE (if running VMs/containers as primary workload). (2) Disk partitioning — recommended layout: boot partition (1GB, ext4), root partition (50-100GB SSD, ext4/xfs), swap (1-2x RAM or 8GB cap), /home (SSD, user data), /var (separate partition for logs/databases, SSD), /data (large HDD pool for bulk storage — mounted separately). Consider LVM for flexible resizing. (3) RAID configuration — if multiple drives: RAID 1 for OS (mirror for redundancy), RAID 5/6 or ZFS raidz1/raidz2 for data pool (capacity with parity), or ZFS mirror pairs. ZFS preferred if RAM allows (1GB per TB of storage). (4) Base config — hostname (neon), static IP on LAN, SSH server (key-only auth, disable password auth, non-standard port optional), firewall (ufw or firewalld — deny all, allow SSH), timezone, NTP sync, automatic security updates (unattended-upgrades). (5) User setup — admin user, sudo group, SSH key deployment from dev machines.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Storage pool setup and mount strategy
sprints.notes: Configure storage pools and mount points for organized data management. Tasks: (1) Create storage pools — if using ZFS: create zpools (tank, fast-pool for SSDs, bulk-pool for HDDs), set compression (lz4), set atime=off, create datasets for each purpose. If using LVM: create volume groups and logical volumes. If using mdadm RAID: create arrays, format, mount. (2) Mount point structure: /data/hexworth/ (Hexworth project repos and working copies), /data/databases/ (database data directories), /data/backups/ (automated backup target), /data/media/ (raw source content — PPTX, PDF, videos), /data/repos/ (forked GitHub repos from Repo Scout), /data/scratch/ (temp workspace for conversions). (3) Permissions — create hexworth group, set proper ownership and permissions on each mount point, ACLs if needed for multi-user access. (4) fstab entries — ensure all mounts persist across reboots with correct options (noatime, nofail for non-critical). (5) Monitoring — set up disk space alerts (df thresholds), SMART monitoring (smartmontools + smartd for drive health alerts), ZFS scrub schedule if using ZFS (monthly). (6) Network shares — Samba share for Windows access from dev machines, NFS for Linux clients, or both. Ensure Hexworth project data is accessible from the WSL development environment.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Database server installation (PostgreSQL + MongoDB)
sprints.notes: Install and configure database servers on Neon. PostgreSQL (relational): (1) Install PostgreSQL 16 (latest stable). (2) Configure postgresql.conf — listen_addresses (LAN IP or 0.0.0.0), port 5432, shared_buffers (25% of RAM), effective_cache_size (75% of RAM), work_mem, maintenance_work_mem, WAL settings for durability. (3) Configure pg_hba.conf — local auth (peer/md5), LAN access (md5/scram-sha-256, restrict to subnet). (4) Create databases: hexworth_prime (Prime platform data), hexworth_arena (Arena game data), hexworth_colosseum (Colosseum game data), hexworth_analytics (usage analytics, progress tracking). (5) Create application user(s) with least-privilege roles. MongoDB (document store): (1) Install MongoDB 7.x Community. (2) Configure mongod.conf — bindIp (LAN), port 27017, storage.dbPath (/data/databases/mongodb), enable authentication. (3) Create databases: hexworth_content (content registry, course materials), hexworth_users (user profiles, progress). (4) Create application users with appropriate roles. Both: (5) Firewall rules — allow DB ports only from trusted LAN IPs. (6) Verify connectivity from dev machines. (7) Basic backup scripts (pg_dump, mongodump) running on cron to /data/backups/.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Network configuration and remote access
sprints.notes: Configure Neon's network for reliable LAN access and optional remote access. LAN setup: (1) Static IP assignment — either static in netplan/NetworkManager or DHCP reservation on router. (2) Hostname resolution — add neon to /etc/hosts on dev machines, or set up local DNS (Pi-hole, dnsmasq) so 'neon' or 'neon.local' resolves from all devices. (3) mDNS/Avahi — install avahi-daemon so neon.local works via mDNS (zero-config). (4) Firewall rules — allow: SSH (22 or custom), PostgreSQL (5432), MongoDB (27017), Samba (445), NFS (2049), HTTP/HTTPS (80/443 for future web services), monitoring (9090 Prometheus, 3000 Grafana). Deny all else. Remote access (optional): (5) Tailscale or WireGuard VPN — secure tunnel for accessing Neon from outside LAN without exposing ports to internet. Tailscale is zero-config; WireGuard is lighter but manual. (6) SSH jump host — if no VPN, SSH on non-standard port with fail2ban for brute-force protection. (7) Dynamic DNS — if ISP gives dynamic IP, set up DDNS (DuckDNS, Cloudflare, No-IP) for consistent remote hostname. (8) Speed test — verify network throughput between dev machines and Neon (iperf3).

sprints.title: Neon Server — Docker and container runtime setup
sprints.notes: Install Docker and container infrastructure on Neon for running services. Tasks: (1) Install Docker Engine (not Docker Desktop — server has no GUI). Add docker group, add admin user to docker group. (2) Install Docker Compose v2 (plugin). (3) Configure Docker — data-root on data drive (not OS drive), default logging driver (json-file with max-size/max-file rotation), DNS settings, default network. (4) Set up docker-compose project structure: /data/hexworth/docker/ with per-service compose files. (5) Initial containers to consider: Portainer (web UI for managing containers), Nginx Proxy Manager or Traefik (reverse proxy for web services), Watchtower (auto-update containers), Uptime Kuma (service monitoring). (6) Container networking — create hexworth-net bridge network for inter-container communication. (7) Volume strategy — named volumes stored on data drives, bind mounts for config files. (8) If databases end up containerized instead of bare-metal (NE-4), set up persistent volumes on data drives with proper backup hooks. Docker gives flexibility to spin up dev/staging environments, run Repo Scout scrapers in containers, or add services like Redis, Elasticsearch, or MinIO later without cluttering the base OS.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Backup strategy and disaster recovery
sprints.notes: Set up automated backups and a disaster recovery plan. Backup targets: (1) Databases — pg_dump (PostgreSQL) and mongodump (MongoDB) nightly to /data/backups/db/ with 7-day rotation. (2) Configuration — /etc/ configs, Docker compose files, cron jobs, firewall rules — backed up weekly. (3) Hexworth project data — git repos are self-backed-up to GitHub, but local working copies and non-git data (raw source content, converted assets, uploaded media) need backup. (4) Backup destination — local backup drive (separate physical drive from data drives), plus off-site: rsync to a cloud storage bucket (Backblaze B2 is cheapest at $5/TB/month), or rsync to a second machine. Tools: (5) restic or borg for deduplicated, encrypted, incremental backups. (6) Cron schedule: databases nightly, full system weekly, configs on change. (7) Backup verification — monthly test restore to confirm backups are valid (untested backups are not backups). (8) Disaster recovery runbook — document: how to rebuild Neon from scratch, where backups live, restore order (OS → storage → databases → services → data), estimated recovery time. Store runbook in the repo, not only on Neon.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Monitoring, alerting, and health dashboard
sprints.notes: Set up monitoring so you know when something goes wrong before it becomes a problem. Stack: (1) Prometheus (metrics collection) — node_exporter for system metrics (CPU, RAM, disk, network, temperature), postgres_exporter for PostgreSQL metrics, mongodb_exporter for MongoDB metrics. (2) Grafana (dashboards) — system overview dashboard (CPU, RAM, disk I/O, network throughput, temperatures), database dashboard (connections, query performance, cache hit ratio, replication lag), Docker dashboard (container status, resource usage), storage dashboard (pool usage, SMART health, ZFS scrub status). (3) Alerting — Grafana alerts or Alertmanager: disk space > 85%, CPU sustained > 90%, RAM > 90%, drive SMART warning, database connection failures, backup job failures, container crash/restart. Notification channels: email, Slack/Discord webhook, or Pushover for mobile push. (4) Uptime Kuma — simple uptime monitor for all services (HTTP endpoints, TCP ports, Docker containers), public status page optional. (5) Log aggregation (optional) — Loki + Promtail for centralized log searching, or simple logrotate + journald for basics. All monitoring services run as Docker containers (NE-6).

sprints.title: Neon Server — Security hardening and access control
sprints.notes: Harden Neon against attack — practice what Hexworth teaches. SSH hardening: (1) Key-only authentication (disable PasswordAuthentication), (2) disable root login, (3) AllowUsers whitelist, (4) fail2ban for brute-force protection (ban after 5 failed attempts, 1-hour ban). Firewall: (5) ufw/firewalld — default deny incoming, explicit allow per service, rate-limit SSH. System hardening: (6) Automatic security updates (unattended-upgrades on Ubuntu/Debian, dnf-automatic on RHEL-based). (7) Remove unnecessary services (telnet, FTP, avahi if not needed). (8) Disable unused network protocols (IPv6 if not used). (9) File integrity monitoring — AIDE or Tripwire for detecting unauthorized changes to system files. (10) AppArmor or SELinux — enforce mandatory access controls. (11) Kernel hardening — sysctl settings (disable IP forwarding unless routing, enable SYN cookies, disable ICMP redirects). (12) User audit — review /etc/passwd, no shared accounts, strong passwords for any non-key accounts. (13) Regular vulnerability scanning — run Lynis audit monthly, review findings. (14) Logging — ensure auditd is running for security event logging, forward logs to centralized location. This is Hexworth's own server — it should be a model of the security practices we teach.

sprints.title: Neon Server — Dev environment integration and workflow connection
sprints.notes: Connect Neon to the daily development workflow so it's actually used, not forgotten. Dev machine integration: (1) Mount Neon shares on WSL — Samba mount in /etc/fstab or systemd automount so /mnt/neon/hexworth is always available. (2) Database connection profiles — set up .pgpass and mongosh connection strings on dev machines for quick DB access. (3) VS Code Remote-SSH — configure VS Code to connect to Neon for editing files directly on server when needed. (4) Git workflow — option A: continue developing locally, push to GitHub, Neon pulls from GitHub (webhook or cron). Option B: develop on Neon via SSH/Remote, push to GitHub from Neon. Option C: local dev + Neon as CI/staging (git push triggers Neon deploy). (5) Repo Scout integration — configure _tools/repo-scout to write discoveries to Neon's database instead of local JSON. (6) Content pipeline — raw source content (PPTX, PDF from EHE, forked repos) stored on Neon's bulk storage, accessed from dev machines via network share. (7) Firebase sync — option to run Firebase CLI from Neon for deployments (firebase deploy from server). (8) Alias/shortcut setup — add ssh aliases and shell functions to .bashrc on dev machines for quick Neon access (ssh neon, neon-db, neon-logs).

sprints.title: User Messaging System — DMs, Inbox, Purge Rules & Moderation
sprints.notes:
Platform-wide user-to-user messaging system. This is the parent epic — see F-23A through F-23F for sub-tasks.

Architecture: Firestore conversation threads pattern. conversations/{convoId} doc (participants[], lastMessage, updatedAt, unreadCount per user) with messages subcollection (sender, text, timestamp, read). This avoids flat message collection query costs and scales well for inbox rendering.

Purge policy: TTL-based (messages auto-delete after 90 days) + cap-based (max 100 messages per conversation, oldest trimmed). Scheduled Cloud Function runs daily purge.

Moderation: This is a B2B educational platform with students. Messaging must have safeguards — handler/instructor visibility option per class, report button, ability to disable messaging per account. This is a policy decision that must be resolved before launch.

Integration points: UserProfileModal (Send Message button), dashboard header (unread badge), FirestoreManager (new methods), firestore.rules (new collections).

Estimate: 3-5x effort of UserProfileModal. Largest feature build to date.

sprints.title: 2-Player Mode for Arcade Games
sprints.notes: Add 2-player options to arcade games. Modes to consider: (1) Split-screen local — two players on same device with split keyboard controls (WASD + arrows). (2) Turn-based — players alternate rounds and compare scores. (3) Real-time multiplayer via Firestore — shared game state, each player sees the other's position/score live. (4) Ghost mode — play against a recorded run from another player. Start with split-screen local or turn-based as MVP since they require no backend changes. Games to target first: Cloud Hop (competitive platforming — who climbs higher), SQL Injection Defense (competitive — who scores higher in same rounds), Don't series games (turn-based score comparison). UI: mode select on start screen (1P / 2P), player indicators, dual score display, winner announcement. Consider: GameTracker integration for 2P stats, leaderboard entries for 2P matches, achievements for multiplayer wins.

sprints.title: Explore Multiplayer Mode for The Hive
sprints.notes: Explore and design multiplayer capabilities for The Hive dungeon crawler. Currently single-player only (solo room navigation, puzzles, Red Queen AI). Multiplayer concepts to explore: (1) Co-op Exploration — 2-4 players navigate the facility together in real-time via Firestore, see each other's positions on the SVG map, collaborate on puzzles, split up to cover more ground. sprints.title: AI Art Pipeline — FAL-Generated Game Assets (Debugger Pilot)
sprints.notes: Establish a FAL (fal.ai) image generation pipeline to produce high-quality game art assets, replacing hand-coded canvas pixel art. Pilot game: shield-debugger.applet.html (F-44 Doom-style FPS) — chosen because raycasting engines live or die by texture quality and enemy sprite variety. PHASE 1 — DEBUGGER PILOT ASSETS: (1) Wall textures — 64x64 or 128x128 tileable textures for each system layer: Userspace (clean server room tiles, fluorescent lighting), Network Stack (cable conduit walls, blinking LEDs), Kernel (raw circuit board traces, capacitor arrays), Firmware (dark metallic plating, warning stripes). Need floor/ceiling textures too. (2) Enemy sprites — each enemy type needs front-facing sprite at minimum, ideally 4-8 angle views for raycasting rotation: Buffer Overflow (bloated glitching mass), Trojan (disguised friendly process + revealed hostile form), Worm (segmented snake-like, multiply animation), Ransomware (padlock-headed enforcer), Zero-Day (glitch/stealth shimmer). Death/pain animation frames for each. (3) Weapon sprites — first-person view-model sprites for each weapon: Firewall Shotgun, Antivirus Rifle, Packet Sniffer Scanner, Sandbox Grenade, IDS Turret, Full Format BFG. Need idle + fire + reload frames. (4) HUD elements — health bar frame, ammo counter, minimap border, threat scanner overlay, pickup item sprites (ammo boxes, health kits = system patches, armor = encryption). (5) Title screen and level transition art. PHASE 2 — PIPELINE STANDARDIZATION: Once Debugger pilot proves the workflow, document the FAL prompt templates, asset size conventions, and color palette rules. Apply pipeline to other games: Root Access (F-45) tile sprites, Runner games (F-42) character/chaser sprites, Flapper games (F-43) obstacle and environment art. TECHNICAL NOTES: FAL supports FLUX, Stable Diffusion, and other models. For pixel art / game sprites, use img2img with pixel art LoRAs or style prompts. Output as PNG sprite sheets, slice into individual frames. Store generated assets in _app/assets/generated/ with source prompts documented. Canvas games load via Image() objects — no build step needed. Consider generating at 2x resolution and downscaling for crisp pixel-perfect rendering on retina displays. SESSION 2026-02-27: Pipeline proven with generate_trophy_medals.py script. Generated 4 trophy/medal icons, 11 FEH module icons, 18 vault module icons, 1 matrix house icon = 34 assets total via fal.ai FLUX.1 [dev].

sprints.title: Messaging — Firestore Data Model & Security Rules
sprints.notes:
Design and implement the Firestore data model for messaging.

Collections:
- conversations/{convoId} — participants[] (2 UIDs), lastMessage (preview text), lastMessageAt (timestamp), unreadCount (map: {uid1: N, uid2: N}), createdAt
- conversations/{convoId}/messages/{msgId} — sender (UID), text (string), timestamp, read (boolean)

Security rules:
- Users can only read/write conversations where their UID is in participants[]
- Messages: sender must match auth.uid on create
- No client delete (only Cloud Functions can purge)
- Rate limit: Cloud Function validates max N messages per hour per user

Indexes:
- conversations: composite index on participants + lastMessageAt (for inbox query)
- messages: timestamp ascending (for chronological thread view)

This is the foundation — all other sub-tasks depend on it.

sprints.title: Messaging — Cloud Functions (send, purge, rate-limit)
sprints.notes:
Server-side messaging logic in functions/index.js.

Functions:
1. sendMessage(recipientUid, text) — validates auth, checks rate limit, sanitizes text (XSS), creates/finds conversation doc, writes message to subcollection, updates lastMessage + unreadCount on conversation doc. Returns convoId.
2. purgeExpiredMessages() — scheduled (daily cron). Deletes messages older than 90 days. Trims conversations over 100 messages (keeps newest). Deletes empty conversations.
3. Rate limiting: max 30 messages per hour per user. Track in users/{uid}/message_rate_limits subcollection (same pattern as flag_attempts).

Considerations:
- Text sanitization (no HTML, max 1000 chars)
- Block list check (if sender is blocked by recipient, reject)
- Notification trigger (could integrate with handler dashboard for class-enrolled students)

sprints.title: Messaging — Client Service (MessagingManager.js)
sprints.notes:

API:
- MessagingManager.sendMessage(recipientUid, text) — calls sendMessage Cloud Function
- MessagingManager.getInbox() — queries conversations where current user is participant, ordered by lastMessageAt desc
- MessagingManager.getThread(convoId) — onSnapshot listener on messages subcollection, ordered by timestamp asc
- MessagingManager.markRead(convoId) — resets unreadCount for current user
- MessagingManager.getUnreadCount() — returns total unread across all conversations (for badge)
- MessagingManager.blockUser(uid) / unblockUser(uid) — writes to user profile blockedUsers[]

Real-time: Use Firestore onSnapshot on conversations collection (filtered by participant) for live unread badge updates. Detach listener on page unload.

Load order: after FirestoreManager, before UI components.

sprints.title: Messaging — Moderation, Reporting & Handler Visibility
sprints.notes:
Moderation layer for student safety on an educational platform.

Requirements:
1. Report button on any message — creates a hed_reports doc (same pattern as existing HED reports) with message content, sender, reporter, conversation context
2. Block user — prevents future messages from that user. Stored in user profile blockedUsers[] array. Cloud Function checks block list before delivering.
3. Handler visibility (configurable per class) — if enabled, handlers can view message activity for their enrolled students. NOT message content by default — just metadata (sent N messages, flagged reports). Full content access only on reported messages.
4. Disable messaging per account — admin can flip a flag to prevent a user from sending messages (abuse response).
5. Content filtering — optional profanity/threat keyword filter on sendMessage Cloud Function. Can be a simple blocklist initially.

Policy decisions needed before implementation:
- Is messaging opt-in or opt-out by default?
- Can handlers see message content or only metadata?
- Age-appropriate messaging restrictions (if platform has minors)?
- Data retention: 90-day TTL adequate for compliance?

sprints.title: Forensics Hub content shows black screen — possible guard/access issue
sprints.notes: FIX: 20 forensics modules (evidence-foundations df-01–10 and disk-forensics df-11–20) loaded AccessGuard.js but never called AccessGuard.require(). AccessGuard auto-injects body{visibility:hidden} on script load, and only showContent() (triggered by require()) removes it. Since require() was never called, body stayed permanently hidden = black screen. Fix: removed unused AccessGuard.js script tags from all 20 modules. ModuleProgress.js unaffected. The other 40 modules (memory/network/log/advanced) correctly use AccessGuard.require('sorted') and work fine.

sprints.title: Investigate prefers-reduced-motion across Hexworth — accessibility compliance for animations

Investigation scope: (1) Audit which pages/components have animations — landing page particles, sorting page effects, mascot two-layer system, CompletionStamp/CLHCompletionModal, HouseRenderer, dashboard transitions, quiz feedback, (2) Determine the right behavior per component: disable entirely, reduce to fade-only, or show static state, (3) Implement via @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) in CSS and matchMedia check in JS for requestAnimationFrame loops, (4) Consider a platform-wide animation toggle in user profile (persisted to localStorage) as a Hexworth-specific override independent of OS setting, (5) Check if this is required for WCAG 2.1 AA compliance (Section 508 / university requirements). The CSS fix is simple per-file but the JS animation loops (particles, typing, mascot) need matchMedia guards. Could also create an EduScan rule to detect requestAnimationFrame or setInterval animation loops without a prefers-reduced-motion check.

sprints.title: CSP hardening — investigate removing unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval
sprints.notes: External pentest flagged CSP weaknesses: script-src allows 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval', style-src allows 'unsafe-inline'. These negate most XSS protection CSP provides. Challenge: Hexworth is 3,503 static HTML files with inline <style> and <script> blocks, no build step. Options to investigate: (1) CSP nonces — Firebase Hosting can inject nonces via Cloud Functions or edge middleware, but requires a serve-time transform for every HTML file, (2) CSP hashes — generate SHA-256 hashes of each inline block and add to CSP header, but hashes change with every edit (maintenance nightmare at scale), (3) Partial removal — remove unsafe-eval from pages that don't need it (~3,450 of 3,503 files don't use eval/Function), keep it only for CodeRunner/SkulptRunner/sandbox pages, (4) Service Worker approach — tenant-sw.js already intercepts HTML responses, could inject nonces at that layer. Scope unsafe-eval first: EduScan HEUR-015 already tracks eval() usage (~50 files). Could create a per-page CSP via meta tag on the ~3,450 safe files that drops unsafe-eval. For unsafe-inline: no realistic path without a build step or serve-time nonce injection.

sprints.title: Crypto-04 AES-ECB Oracle — move secret server-side to prevent View Source bypass
sprints.notes: The AES-ECB byte-at-a-time oracle challenge (arena/boxes/crypto-04-aes-ecb/config.js) has the secret payload ('SECRET_PAYLOAD_') hardcoded in client-side JavaScript. Students can skip the entire cryptanalysis challenge by reading the source. Fix: create a Cloud Function oracle endpoint that appends the secret server-side and returns only ciphertext blocks. The client sends the chosen plaintext prefix, the server appends the secret, encrypts with AES-ECB, and returns the ciphertext. Student never sees the secret — they must recover it byte-by-byte through the oracle, which is the whole point of the challenge.

sprints.title: SSH Sandbox — Phase 1: Container Prep (bc1/bc2/bc3)
sprints.notes: Add openssh-server to all 4 Docker images (terminal-light, terminal-full, ide, postgres-lab). Write entrypoint-ssh.sh for credential bootstrapping. Write SSH banner. Add lab tools (nmap, netcat, tmux, etc.) to terminal-full. Configure sshd_config. Build and test locally. Work happens on bc1/bc2/bc3 in hexworth-sandbox/ repo. Scope doc: _planning/SSH_SANDBOX_SCOPE.md section 3.3 + 5. Est: 1-2 days.

sprints.title: SSH Sandbox — Phase 2: WebSocket Bridge (Cloud Run)
sprints.notes: Create Cloud Run ssh-bridge service (Node.js + ws + ssh2 + firebase-admin). WebSocket server validates Firebase ID token, looks up Firestore session, opens SSH to container, pipes bidirectional I/O. Handle resize events, 30s reconnection grace period. Deploy to Cloud Run. Work in hexworth-sandbox/ssh-bridge/. Scope doc: _planning/SSH_SANDBOX_SCOPE.md section 7.1. Est: 2-3 days.

sprints.title: SSH Sandbox — Phase 3: Frontend Integration (SandboxLauncher.js)
sprints.notes: Add xterm.js + addons to SandboxLauncher.js. Build tab UI (Web Terminal / SSH Terminal / Connection Info). Credential display with copy buttons. Wire xterm.js to WebSocket bridge. Add Extend Session button + API call. Update session timer. Update LAB_INFO with sshEnabled flag. This phase touches hexworth-prime repo. Scope doc: _planning/SSH_SANDBOX_SCOPE.md section 6. Est: 1-2 days.

sprints.title: SSH Sandbox — Phase 4: Native SSH via Cloudflare Tunnel
sprints.notes: Configure Cloudflare Tunnel for SSH protocol. Wildcard DNS *.ssh-lab.hexworth.dev. Cloudflare Access app with Firebase as IdP. Traefik TCP router for SSH port routing. Test with and without cloudflared client. Document student setup. Can run parallel with Phase 2. Work on bc1/bc2/bc3. Scope doc: _planning/SSH_SANDBOX_SCOPE.md section 3.2 + Phase 4. Est: 1 day.

sprints.title: SSH Sandbox — Phase 5: Instructor Dashboard + Cleanup
sprints.notes: Add Live Lab Sessions panel to InstructorDashboard.js (real-time Firestore listener). Session duration tracking, CSV export extension. Add cleanupExpiredSessions Cloud Function (scheduled every 5 min). Firestore security rules for ssh_sessions. Touches hexworth-prime: InstructorDashboard.js, functions/index.js, firestore.rules, firestore.indexes.json. Scope doc: _planning/SSH_SANDBOX_SCOPE.md section 8 + Phase 5. Est: 1 day.

sprints.title: Tiered alerts — Cloud Function watcher for runtime monitor failures
sprints.notes:
Currently runtime monitor (Cloud Run, every 15 min) writes results to Cloud Logging only — failures sit there until someone looks. Build alert plumbing: Cloud Function triggered by Cloud Logging entries where jsonPayload.allPassed=false. Send tiered alerts: Pulse dashboard refresh (passive), push notification (medium), email via SendGrid/Mailgun (high — prod-down level). Decision points: which severity triggers which channel; rate-limiting (alert storm prevention); on-call rotation. DEPLOY.md has the basic Firestore-write upgrade pattern; alerts build on top.

Awaiting user direction.

sprints.title: CLH course three-layer investigation — content + key-architecture audit
sprints.notes:
Surfaced 2026-05-05 attempting Block A of SYM-15 (the 13 CLH PROG-003 collisions). Discovered THREE file layers per CLH slot, not two:

1. Layer A — old applets at script/clh/script-clh-NNN-intro.applet.html (key: script-clh-NNN-intro). Topics MATCH the hub's canonical MODULES array.

2. Layer B — course modules at script/courses/clh/modules/clh-NNN/script-intro.module.html (same key as A). Topics DIFFER from hub — appears to be off-by-N drift, possibly from an earlier curriculum version that never re-aligned.

3. Layer C — linux applets at script/applets/linux/script-clh-NNN-<topic>.applet.html using uppercase 'CLH-NNN' key format. 19 files (CLH-001..019), unclear whether parallel curriculum or duplicate.

The original 'rename applets' plan was structurally wrong: (a) hub has a hardcoded migration shim at lines 442-468 of script/courses/clh/index.html that assumes script-clh-NNN-intro key shape — renaming applets breaks hub progress display for completing students, (b) topic-derived applet keys would semantically collide with layer C, (c) needs 4-system change minimum.

Full investigation doc: _docs/operations/sym-17-clh-three-layer-investigation.md.

What needs to happen:
- Curriculum-owner verification that hub MODULES array is canonical for 2026
- Per-slot decision on layer B course modules: stale (move/retire), intentional alternate (rename), or wrong-content (fix to match slot)
- Layer C scope decision: parallel Linux track, duplicate, or retire
- Hub migration shim expansion if new keys need coverage
- Then code work: renames + cross-credit shims with correct destinations

Not autonomous — curriculum review required. PROG-003 baseline currently sits at 13 (the CLH bucket) until this resolves.

CLH = Command Line Hacker. Self-contained course in House of Script with own hub. 30 modules across foundation/operations/analysis/capstone tiers.

--- 2026-05-08 NANCY VERIFICATION (HEUR-025 Strategy 2 demotion attempt blocked) ---

Nancy verification gate during HEUR-025 Strategy 2 demotion proposal CONFIRMED CLH ongoing write-pattern drift extends to recent files. Sample of clh-020 through clh-028 (April 2026 builds): EVERY one calls `ModuleProgress.complete('script', 'script-clh-NNN-intro', ...)` — the legacy format. The CLH module template was never updated to write canonical clh-NNN keys.

The migration shim at hub lines 433-473 is masking AN ONGOING WRITE-PATTERN DRIFT, not just preserving legacy student data. New completions from CLH-027 etc. ALSO depend on the shim to surface in the hub.

PROG-003 baseline updated: 14 CLH-bucket findings (was 13) per latest nexus scan; one new collision since SYM-17 was opened (likely a new CLH module added after sprint creation).

This confirms SYM-17's premise: the convention drift is system-wide, not historical-only. Curriculum-owner verification still required before code work — but the urgency increased: every new CLH module ships with the drift baked in. Suggest stub a CLH module template change (write canonical key) as Block 0 of SYM-17 even before per-slot architecture decisions.

sprints.title: Build slide-split automation tool — closes QC-38 fix path
sprints.description: QC-38 fix work needs automation: 1,199 slides across 153 files need iterative split-measure-resplit cycles. Manual editorial pass = ~150 hours; per-file CSS density means simple in-half splits don't always fit (proved this 2026-05-06 with cloud-cse-module01 attempt: 3+3 split made overflow worse, not better). Build _tools/slide-splitter/auto-split.js that uses OVERFLOW-001 detector in a feedback loop: parse slide HTML, identify natural split points (grid items, list items, sub-headings, paragraph-after-heading), try splits of increasing granularity, measure each candidate via headless browser, apply smallest split that fits within 612px container. Default mode: dry-run (output proposed splits as diff). --apply flag writes. Renumber slide-of-N labels file-wide automatically. Titles use '(Part N)' suffix v0.5; editorial pass refines titles in v1. Single-file initially; batch mode v1.
sprints.notes: v0.5 SHIPPED 2026-05-06 (commit 49891d99). _tools/slide-splitter/auto-split.js. Demo run on cloud-cse-module01 (23 overflows): auto-fixed 5 (22%), 13 NO-CONVERGE (need content reduction not splitting — chrome overhead per slide too large), 5 UNSPLITTABLE (bespoke). Confirms QC-38 fix scope is bigger than 'just split': for chunky-card files, need content density reduction. Oracle has known v1 issue: some candidates pass oracle then re-overflow post-write — investigation deferred. v1 plan: (a) tighter oracle parity with OVERFLOW-001 detector, (b) atom-density-aware balancing, (c) semantic title pass via LLM agent.

sprints.title: Pulse Self-Healing — Visibility Layer (post-Nancy revision: UI wire-up only)
sprints.notes:
REVISED 2026-05-08 after Nancy adversarial review (PAUSE verdict on initial proposal). Scope reduced to a single targeted change: extend the existing systemStatusLine in _app/pulse.html (line ~608) Self-Healing System panel to surface, FROM EXISTING DATA only:
- _auto_fix_queue depth (queue length)
- timestamp of most recent _auto_fix_queue history[] entry where actor.startsWith('agent:') (= last apply by an agent)
- _quality_reports/scanHeartbeat.scannedAt freshness (scan recency)
- _system_config/self_healing master toggle state
- 'Run nexus autofix-dryrun for promotion candidates' CTA (terminal command, not UI button)

Nancy's three blocking concerns on the original proposal (must NOT be reintroduced without resolution):
1. The 1-click Promote button has no safe implementation. Firestore overlay = scan-pipeline hot-path Firestore read (architectural change). CF-pushes-commit = deploy-gate violation. Stays manual: edit publish.js + redeploy.
2. The state banner originally proposed _system_config/auto_healer_state written by 'the apply CF on every cycle' — but no scheduled apply CF exists today. autofix-apply is a manual CLI. Banner must derive state from _auto_fix_queue.history[] + scanHeartbeat, not from a new doc.
3. N=10 sample dry-run is structurally weaker than the existing autofix-dryrun command (full corpus). Promotion eligibility scanner = duplicate work at lower fidelity. Skip the scanner; surface the existing CLI.

Missing scope Nancy flagged that this sprint MUST add:
- IDLE-READY ambiguity: distinguish 'queue confirmed empty 4min ago' from 'no scan in 3 days' using scanHeartbeat freshness.
- APPLY-ERROR-SPIKE detection: if ≥3 consecutive history[] entries show validated:false in last 30min, render red state.
- Reaper health: surface 'reaper last ran X min ago' separately from healer state (distinct signals).

Deliverable: ~50-line patch to pulse.html + TriageQueueClient.js. No new Firestore docs. No new CFs. No new scanner. Pure visibility from existing data.

User pushback that triggered this: 'you were just in idle waiting for I don't know what? there is no notification or label on the auto heal area letting me know what is going on.'

sprints.title: Auto-Healing Pipeline Hardening (de-promotion + auto-promote burn-in — Phase 2)
sprints.notes:
REVISED 2026-05-08 to incorporate Nancy's blocking concern: 'No de-promotion mechanism exists. Cannot add Promote button without de-promotion.' Phase 2 scope expanded:

(1) DE-PROMOTION (blocking, must ship before any auto-promote):
  - Detect ≥3 consecutive validated:false history entries on a promoted rule
  - Auto-flip per-template enable to OFF in _system_config/self_healing
  - Write critical-severity item to _triage_queue tagged auto-disabled-rule
  - Master toggle still works as kill-all

(2) AUTO-PROMOTE ON BURN-IN (deferred until ≥3 promoted rules with months of clean operating history):
  - Auto-add rule to AUTO_FIX_ELIGIBLE_RULES when (a) template + validator pair exists, (b) full autofix-dryrun PASSes against current findings, (c) zero validator failures over a cooldown window
  - Audit-logged with operator review window before activation
  - Currently blocked: only CAT-002 promoted, insufficient operating history

(3) APPLY()-EDIT INTEGRITY (Nancy concern #4): apply() uses regex-based string edit on ContentCatalog.js, not AST-aware. Insertion can be syntactically valid but semantically wrong (e.g., wrong outer-array close). Validator post-write parse may pass even on corruption. Mitigation options: (a) AST-aware insertion via @babel/parser, (b) snapshot-diff sanity check (post-apply file size delta within expected range), (c) integration test that purposely passes a malformed catalog to confirm rollback fires.

Depends on: PULSE-1 (visibility prerequisite — operator must be able to SEE failures before automation increases).

sprints.title: Dashboard tenant-mode encapsulation — fix HEUR-014 onclick bypass (18 findings)
sprints.notes:
EduScan HEUR-014 finds 18 hardcoded onclick redirects in _app/dashboard.html (lines ~5945-5990). Each is a mini-house-card with both `href="..."` (invalid on a div) and `onclick="window.location.href='...'"`. These bypass TenantRouter.getUrl() which would redirect tenant users to their hub instead of letting them navigate Hexworth-internal pages.

Dashboard.html has AccessGuard but no tenant-mode check — a tenant user could land here and the onclicks would take them to arctic/, arena/, hive/, etc.

Fix options:
  A. Add TenantRouter.isActive() check at top of dashboard.html; redirect tenant users to TenantRouter.getHubUrl() before render. Single-file fix, defends every nav element.
  B. Replace each onclick with TenantRouter-aware navigation. Multi-line, but preserves dashboard usability for non-tenant.
  C. Combine: A as defense-in-depth, B as belt-and-braces.

Recommend: A (4-line fix at top of dashboard.html) since dashboard is Hexworth-internal-only by design. The 18 onclicks become moot if tenant users never reach the page.

Alternative: HEUR-014 validator may itself be over-firing — the destination URLs ARE correct for non-tenant users, and tenant users shouldn't hit dashboard.html in the first place. If A is implemented, the HEUR-014 finding could be downgraded to info via validator update.

Reference: TenantRouter API at _app/components/TenantRouter.js (getUrl, getHubUrl, isActive, goToHub).

---

## Nancy Review 2026-05-08 — VERDICT: PAUSE

Proposed surgical fix (TenantRouter check + `window.location.replace` in <head>) reviewed by adversarial agent. Three concerns:

**1. AccessGuard double-load fragility (medium)**: AccessGuard.js line 1025-1029 dynamically injects `<script src='/components/TenantRouter.js'>` for any tenant user. The proposed static load makes that dynamic injection branch never fire. The coupling is undocumented; reverting the static load would break AccessGuard's auto-load expectations on other pages.

**2. BLOCKING: admin-with-stale-tenant lockout (high)**: A developer or instructor who tested a tenant flow has `hexworth_tenant` localStorage data. After the fix, they get redirected to the tenant hub on EVERY visit to dashboard.html, BEFORE Firebase auth resolves and BEFORE AccessGuard's admin bypass runs. There is NO `clearTenant()` method in TenantRouter.js. No `removeItem('hexworth_tenant')` path exists in the codebase. There is no documented escape hatch.

**3. Analytics v2 partial-load (low)**: `window.location.replace` from `<head>` fires before Firebase analytics SDK loads. Produces partial page-load events; possibly visible to runtime monitor at hexworth.com (live since 2026-05-04).

**Resolution required before shipping**:
- Add `?notenant` URL param bypass to the redirect: `&& !location.search.includes('notenant')` — admin/developer can append `?notenant` to escape
- AND/OR add a `clearTenant()` method to TenantRouter.js that removes both sessionStorage and localStorage `hexworth_tenant` keys, surfaced in admin UI (e.g., a 'Switch Off Tenant Mode' menu item)
- AND audit the `_tenant.branding.dashboardVariant` resolution path in TenantRouter.js:62 to confirm it gracefully handles malformed/stale JSON (does `/tenant/index.html?slug=<missing>` 404 or render?)

Until these are resolved: defer fix. Sprint stays in backlog.

Alternative: validator-side fix to HEUR-014 — recognize that dashboard.html is Hexworth-internal and the onclicks are correct for non-tenant users. Downgrade severity. Tracked as a sub-option under ES-1115 if convention-aware validator design is pursued.

sprints.title: A+ Core 1 prep-rounds — client-grading violation + orphan static keys
sprints.notes:
DETECTED 2026-05-08 via OPT-COUNT-MISMATCH scan + manual code review.

FOUR cert-prep quizzes for CompTIA A+ Core 1 are using CLIENT-SIDE grading, violating the platform mandate (memory feedback_cert_hubs_server_graded.md): 'ALL cert hub quizzes MUST use server-side grading — no client-side scoring'.

Files:

  - _app/houses/forge/applets/comptia-aplus/core-1/quizzes/forge-aplus-core1-prep-round-2.quiz.html
  - _app/houses/forge/applets/comptia-aplus/core-1/quizzes/forge-aplus-core1-prep-round-3.quiz.html
  - _app/houses/forge/applets/comptia-aplus/core-1/quizzes/forge-aplus-core1-prep-round-4.quiz.html

Each uses an inline custom quiz engine (not QuizEngine class) with `var passed = pct >= CONFIG.passingScore;` — answers compared CLIENT-SIDE in browser. Students can inspect/modify CONFIG.questions and trivially game the score.

ALSO: Static answer keys are misnamed and stale:
  - HTML moduleId: 'aplus-core1-prep-r1' (and r2/r3/r4)
  - Static key:    'forge-aplus-core1-prep-r1' (and r2/r3/r4) ← orphan
  - Static answer count: 4 (per quiz)
  - HTML question count: 10 (per quiz)

If converted to server-grading without renaming, lookup misses → 0/10 silent fail.

FIX SCOPE (per-quiz):
  1. Refactor quiz to use QuizEngine pattern (replace inline rendering)
  2. Set serverGrading: true, achievement, moduleId, etc.
  3. Generate correct answer array (10 entries) from current CONFIG.questions correctAnswer fields
  4. Add static entry under correct key 'aplus-core1-prep-r1' (matches HTML moduleId)
  5. Reseed Firestore quiz_keys/aplus-core1-prep-r1
  6. Run verify-quiz-keys.js per ID
  7. Karl Mode-2 audit on each prep round
  8. EduScan + smoke gate
  9. Atomic deploy: ./deploy.sh + reseed in same authorized op

IMPACT: Currently students completing these prep rounds get a client-computed pass/fail with no audit trail and no integrity. Cert prep tracks need server-grading to be exam-quality.

BLOCKING: hex Forge house has active A+ Core 1 cohorts. Refactor must preserve question content and option-order so existing student progress (localStorage CONFIG.storageKey) doesn't reset spuriously.

DEPS: None hard. Soft: aligns with template refactor work in pending task #46 (server-graded pattern demonstrator already exists in templates/quiz-template.html).

All 4 prep-rounds already carry `<html data-practice-mode="true">` (verified). EduScan QUIZ-002 validator (heuristics.js:1276) explicitly demotes severity HIGH -> MEDIUM when this marker is present. Current state: 4 QUIZ-002 in MEDIUM bucket, 0 in HIGH bucket. Working as designed via the severity-demotion pattern.

Clearing them entirely is BLOCKED on architectural lift, not a simple refactor:
  - Each prep-round is multi-modal: 4 MC + 3 GUI hotspot + 3 terminal-input questions
  - gradeQuiz CF only handles MC. GUI/terminal modalities have no server-grading path on the platform today.
  - Closing the QUIZ-002 entirely needs either (a) extend gradeQuiz CF for gui/terminal, or (b) split each prep-round into a server-graded MC quiz + a separate client-side practice applet. Both are platform-wide design conversations, not bounded refactors.

The "FIX SCOPE" section above (steps 1-9) was written assuming a vanilla MC client-grading violation. That framing is wrong: the practice-mode marker is already applied, and the 4 questions per round that ARE MC could in principle be migrated, but the GUI/terminal questions cannot follow the same pattern.

Reclassification: HIGH "refactor 4 quizzes" -> DESIGN "multi-modal server-grading pattern". sprints.notes:
DETECTED 2026-05-08 via platform-wide grading-pattern scan.

**95 quizzes** in `_app/` use client-side grading (`q.ans` or `correct: N` field with no `gradeQuiz`/`serverGrading`). Violates feedback_cert_hubs_server_graded.md mandate. Students can View Source to see answers OR submit any answer with client saying 'pass'.

**Distribution by track (count: path):**
  - 16: houses/divergent/cybersecurity-policy/quizzes (CIS Cybersecurity Policy)
  -  8: houses/web/net-essentials/quizzes (CIS Networking Essentials cr-w*)
  -  8: houses/web/intro-networks/quizzes (Foundations of Networking fl-w*)
  -  8: houses/script/linux-essentials/quizzes
  -  8: houses/forge/server-management/quizzes
  -  8: houses/forge/hardware-support/quizzes
  -  8: houses/code/python-programming/quizzes
  -  8: houses/cloud/cloud-essentials/quizzes
  -  4: houses/shield/infosec/quizzes
  -  4: houses/forge/applets/comptia-aplus/core-1/quizzes (covered by QC-54)
  -  4: houses/divergent/cybersecurity-ethics/quizzes (cse-w2/w3/w4 covered by QC-56)
  -  4: houses/cloud/openstack/quizzes
  -  3: houses/divergent/ethics-it/quizzes (eth-w1/w2/w3 covered by QC-56)
  -  3: houses/code/python-for-it/quizzes (active COP1034C track)
  -  1: houses/web/network-plus/quizzes

**Two patterns observed:**
  - Pattern A: `"ans": N` in question objects + inline `selectAnswer(idx) { if (idx === q.ans) ...}` (eth/cse/cr/fl/etc. weekly format)
  - Pattern B: `correct: N` + similar (openstack)

**Sub-sprints already filed for slices:**
  - QC-54: A+ Core 1 prep-rounds (4 quizzes)
  - QC-56: Divergent weekly (eth-w + cse-w, 6 quizzes)

**Remaining: 85 quizzes** outside QC-54+QC-56 scope.

**FIX TEMPLATE (per quiz):**
  1. Refactor inline grading to QuizEngine pattern
  2. serverGrading: true, randomize: true, achievement, moduleId
  3. Schema migration: `{q, opts, ans, exp}` -> `{question, options, explanation}` (drop ans)
  4. Generate answer array from existing ans values
  5. Add static entry under correct moduleId
  6. Reseed Firestore (production-write gate per quiz batch)
  7. Karl Mode-2 audit
  8. EduScan + smoke gate
  9. Atomic deploy

**Sequencing recommendation:**
  1. Active courses first (python-for-it, CIS2253 cybersecurity-ethics, cybersecurity-policy)
  2. Cert prep tracks (A+/Network+/Linux+)
  3. General/elective

**EduScan gap:** existing QUIZ-002 (`correct: N` without serverGrading) catches Pattern B but not Pattern A (`q.ans`). Validator extension would surface this class proactively. NOT a blocker for the cleanup; could be addressed as part of QC-57 follow-up.

**Total impact:** roughly 95 × 10-15 questions = ~1,000-1,400 active quiz questions are gameable.

sprints.notes:

Full inventory: `_docs/operations/qc-60-hub-catalog-mismatch-inventory.md`

**Top affected hubs:**

  102 - matrix/protocore (100% miss)

   16 - eye/cysa (100% miss)

   ... (19 hubs total)

**Reference cases (sub-sprints):**
  - QC-59 (PFI 33 genuine missing): SHIPPED via commit f69acd66 — added entries (PFI catalog already used bare-ID convention).
  - QC-47 (PIS 21 prefix-mismatch): held pending Nancy review on student-progress-data implications.

**IMPACT** — affects active student-facing courses across:
  - CIS courses (cybersecurity, networking, etc.)
  - Cert prep tracks (Security+, Network+, Linux+, A+, CySA+, ISC2-CC, etc.)
  - Microsoft cert paths (AZ-104, AZ-900, MS-102, MS-900, SC-200, SC-900, PL-300)

  - Specialty (eye/cysa, adv-linux, sql)

**FIX STRATEGY (per option):**
  A. Mass-rename catalog: drop `${house}-` prefix from all 483 prefixed entries. Single direction. Risk: any code using prefixed IDs breaks; student-progress data may be keyed under prefixed IDs.
  B. Mass-update hub data-modules: add `${house}-` prefix to all 483 hub references. Risk: 500+ HTML edits across 19 hubs; future authors don't expect prefix.
  C. Add bare-ID aliases: 483 NEW catalog entries with bare IDs pointing to same hrefs. Risk: triggers CAT-007 dual-naming on 483 entries (massive eduscan finding noise).
  D. Define canonical convention in `_docs/architecture/`: BARE for hub data-module + catalog id. Migrate via tooling that updates both, with student-progress migrateLegacyKey calls per affected ID.

**Recommended:** Option D + a coordinated migration sprint per house. Don't attempt mass-fix in one commit.

For genuinely missing (17): same pattern as QC-59 — add entries mechanically. Smaller scope, can be done first as quick win:

Deep-dive into matrix/adv-linux ('14 genuinely missing' subset) revealed that several of those modules ALREADY have catalog entries with BOTH a prefix AND a suffix (e.g. hub uses `ala-w1-network-config` but catalog has `matrix-ala-w1-network-config-pres`). The original audit's `endsWith('-' + bareId)` heuristic missed these because the suffix `-pres` extends past the bareId.

Mixed conventions exist within the SAME house:

  - `id: 'matrix-ala-w1-cli-operations-pres'` (prefixed+suffixed, category: 'adv-linux', icon: desktop)
  Both for the SAME content file. Already CAT-007 dual-naming.

IMPLICATION: The 'genuinely missing 17' subset is NOT actually a clean QC-59-style mechanical fix. The convention mess includes:

  - prefix+suffix mismatches
  - dual-entry CAT-007 cases
  - and yes, some genuine missing

Quick-win matrix/adv-linux fix is BLOCKED on convention decision. Same for cyber-framework mm06/mm07/mm08 (3 files don't exist on filesystem — different bug class entirely).

sprints.title: PIS presentation progress-key mismatch — 17 short-key writers vs hub long-key checks
sprints.notes:
DETECTED 2026-05-08 via Nancy adversarial review of QC-47 catalog rename. Pre-existing bug, surfaced but NOT closed by the catalog rename.

The 17 PIS presentation files at _app/houses/shield/infosec/presentations/pis-w*-*.presentation.html call ModuleProgress.complete() with SHORTER keys than the hub's `weeks` progress array expects, breaking completion-checkmark display.

Examples confirmed by Nancy:
  - pis-w1-cia-triad.presentation.html line 1457: `ModuleProgress.complete('shield', 'pis-w1-cia', ...)` — hub expects 'pis-w1-cia-triad'
  - pis-w1-security-controls.presentation.html: `ModuleProgress.complete('shield', 'pis-w1-controls', ...)` — hub expects 'pis-w1-security-controls'
  - pis-w1-threat-actors.presentation.html: `ModuleProgress.complete('shield', 'pis-w1-threats', ...)` — hub expects 'pis-w1-threat-actors'
  - pis-w1-social-engineering.presentation.html: `ModuleProgress.complete('shield', 'pis-w1-social', ...)` — hub expects 'pis-w1-social-engineering'
  - pis-w1-malware.presentation.html: `ModuleProgress.complete('shield', 'pis-w1-malware', ...)` — MATCHES (only one of W1)
  - pis-w4-identity-management.presentation.html line 1311: `ModuleProgress.complete('shield', 'pis-w4-identity-mgmt', ...)` — hub expects 'pis-w4-identity-management'

**Audit needed**: full inventory of all 17 presentations to enumerate which match the hub keys and which don't. Nancy verified ≥5 mismatches in W1 + W4; W2/W3 unaudited.

**Impact**: students who complete a presentation see no checkmark in the hub. Progress IS recorded in localStorage under the short key — it's just not surfaced via the hub UI. Existing student data is durable and would need migrateLegacyKey shim if the keys are normalized.

**Fix scope (per Nancy's recommended order)**:
  1. Inventory: grep all 17 presentation files for ModuleProgress.complete() second arg, build mismatch table
  2. Decide canonical: which side is wrong — short keys (terse, presentation-author choice) or long keys (full module ID, hub's expectation, matches catalog)?
  3. Migration: if long keys are canonical, add migrateLegacyKey('pis-w1-cia', 'pis-w1-cia-triad') etc. for student data preservation
  4. Update presentation files to write the canonical key
  5. EduScan + verify hub checkmarks render after browser reload with prior localStorage

**Convention question**: short keys appear chosen for terseness; long keys appear chosen for ID alignment. If presentations across the platform follow the short-key convention, this could affect more than just PIS — needs platform-wide check before normalizing.

**Discovered while auditing QC-47** — the 21-prefix-strip restored hub-to-catalog metadata lookup but did NOT fix the progress-display checkmarks. Surfaced in commit (TBD) of QC-47 catalog rename.

DEPS: None hard. Soft: aligns with reference_module_progress_migrate_legacy_key.md memory pattern (one-time migration shim for renaming progress keys without orphaning student data).

--- 2026-05-08 FULL INVENTORY (step #1 complete) ---

All 17 PIS presentation files audited. 7 mismatches, 10 already-correct.

MISMATCHES (7) — presentation writes short key, hub expects long key:
  | presentation file                          | writes              | hub expects                    |
  |--------------------------------------------|---------------------|--------------------------------|
  | pis-w1-cia-triad.presentation.html         | pis-w1-cia          | pis-w1-cia-triad               |
  | pis-w1-security-controls.presentation.html | pis-w1-controls     | pis-w1-security-controls       |
  | pis-w1-social-engineering.presentation.html| pis-w1-social       | pis-w1-social-engineering      |
  | pis-w1-threat-actors.presentation.html     | pis-w1-threats      | pis-w1-threat-actors           |
  | pis-w3-network-architecture.presentation.html | pis-w3-network-arch | pis-w3-network-architecture    |
  | pis-w3-security-operations.presentation.html  | pis-w3-sec-ops      | pis-w3-security-operations     |
  | pis-w4-identity-management.presentation.html  | pis-w4-identity-mgmt| pis-w4-identity-management     |

ALREADY-CORRECT (10): pis-w1-malware, pis-w2-app-attacks, pis-w2-cryptography, pis-w2-device-security, pis-w2-network-attacks, pis-w3-pki, pis-w3-wireless-cloud, pis-w4-authentication, pis-w4-incident-response, pis-w4-risk-governance.

PATTERN: W1 was authored with terse short keys (4 of 5 are short, malware was short by coincidence). W2 was authored with full keys (4/4). W3 mixed (2 short + 2 full). W4 mostly full with one abbreviation (identity-mgmt). Looks like the convention shifted between W1 and W2 — likely the convention got formalized to long-keys = filename mid-build, and the W1 + a few stragglers were never updated.

CANONICAL: long keys (match presentation filename + hub expectation + ContentCatalog ID after QC-47 rename). Already enforced by 10 of 17. Normalize the other 7.

FIX (next step):
  1. Edit 7 presentation files: change ModuleProgress.complete() second arg from short to long key.
  2. Add migrateLegacyKey shim calls for the 7 short keys (per reference_module_progress_migrate_legacy_key.md):
     - migrateLegacyKey('pis-w1-cia', 'pis-w1-cia-triad')
     - migrateLegacyKey('pis-w1-controls', 'pis-w1-security-controls')
     - migrateLegacyKey('pis-w1-social', 'pis-w1-social-engineering')
     - migrateLegacyKey('pis-w1-threats', 'pis-w1-threat-actors')
     - migrateLegacyKey('pis-w3-network-arch', 'pis-w3-network-architecture')
     - migrateLegacyKey('pis-w3-sec-ops', 'pis-w3-security-operations')
     - migrateLegacyKey('pis-w4-identity-mgmt', 'pis-w4-identity-management')
  3. Place migrations early in ModuleProgress.init or via a one-time calling pattern (see existing migrateLegacyKey usages).
  4. Test: load hub with localStorage containing a short-key entry; checkmark should display under the long key.
  5. EduScan + smoke gate.

*Pre-existing similar pattern check still TODO*: are short keys also used by presentations OUTSIDE shield/infosec? If yes, this is a platform-wide normalization, not a PIS-only fix. Marathon backlog item: scan all *.presentation.html for ModuleProgress.complete() second arg vs filename.

--- 2026-05-08 PHASE 1 COMPLETE (write-keys, no migration) ---

Nancy second review on the Phase 1 plan PAUSED on two issues:

  (1) The 7 long keys are referenced in THREE hubs (infosec, security-plus, isc2-cc), not just infosec. A migration block in only one hub leaves students using security-plus or isc2-cc with stranded short keys.

  (2) FirestoreManager cloud-sync (syncBidirectional, FirestoreManager.js:1240) re-restores cloud-stored short keys to localStorage on every page load. Adding migrateLegacyKey blocks would create a ping-pong: migration runs (deletes short), cloud sync runs (re-adds short), repeat. NET WORSE than current state.

Decision: ship Phase 1 = WRITE-KEY EDITS ONLY (no migration block). Strictly better than current state:
  - New students: writes long key, hub displays checkmark, cloud has long key.
  - Existing students with short-key cloud data: hub still does not show checkmark unless they re-complete (same as today). State preserved, no regression.
  - Zero new bugs introduced.

Applied to 7 files:
  - pis-w1-cia-triad.presentation.html (was pis-w1-cia)
  - pis-w1-security-controls.presentation.html (was pis-w1-controls)
  - pis-w1-social-engineering.presentation.html (was pis-w1-social)
  - pis-w1-threat-actors.presentation.html (was pis-w1-threats)
  - pis-w3-network-architecture.presentation.html (was pis-w3-network-arch)
  - pis-w3-security-operations.presentation.html (was pis-w3-sec-ops)
  - pis-w4-identity-management.presentation.html (was pis-w4-identity-mgmt)

Verification post-edit: 17/17 PIS presentations now write keys matching their filename + hub data-module.

--- DEFERRED: PHASE 2 + PHASE 3 ---

Phase 2 (cloud-side migration): design how to migrate Firestore profile data (modulesCompleted) from short to long keys without ping-pong. Options:
  (a) Server-side migrator: one-time admin script that rewrites user profile docs (find+replace 7 short keys to long keys in modulesCompleted/labsCompleted arrays).
  (b) recordProgress CF gate: alias-aware, rewrites short-to-long on read.
  (c) Client-side migration AFTER syncBidirectional completes — runs migrateLegacyKey post-cloud-sync, then re-syncs back. Tricky with offline edge cases.

Phase 3 (existing-student backfill): for any student whose cloud profile has only the short key, surface a one-time prompt or auto-complete the long-key version after Phase 2 lands.

Nancy re-review required before Phase 2 design ships. Production-write authorization required for Phase 2 (admin script touches all user profile docs).

sprints.title: Server+ M10 Group Policy — single file backs two distinct hub cards (architectural decision)
sprints.notes:
DETECTED 2026-05-08 during HEUR-025 platform-wide bulk-fix (commit 721c9fb4). The fix script's pre-flight dual-target detection excluded one file from the 80-finding Strategy 1 batch; m10 needs operator decision before fix.

**File**: `_app/houses/cloud/modules/wsa/m10-group-policy/cloud-presentation.module.html`

**Single complete() call** (line 886): `ModuleProgress.complete('cloud', 'cloud-wsa-m10-presentation', ...)`

**TWO hub cards reference this file** in `_app/houses/cloud/server-plus/index.html`:
  - L221: `data-module="wsa-m10-pres"` — "Group Policy / GPOs, preferences, security policies"
  - L255: `data-module="wsa-m10-sec"`  — "Group Policy Security / Security policies, audit, password policies"

Both cards link to the SAME file. Two distinct learning cards, one piece of content. No matter what write-key the file uses, exactly ONE of the two cards gets a checkmark (or neither).

**Options for operator decision** (no unilateral action — content architecture call):

  A. **Split file** — clone `cloud-presentation.module.html` into two distinct files: `m10-group-policy-overview.module.html` (writes `wsa-m10-pres`) + `m10-group-policy-security.module.html` (writes `wsa-m10-sec`). Update hub hrefs. Each card gets independent completion + content can diverge.

  B. **Multi-key write** — file calls `ModuleProgress.complete()` twice (once with each hub-key). Both cards get checkmark on completion. Risk: mixes two semantically distinct module IDs in one file, may confuse student-progress analytics; doubles XP if XP is per-call.
